text: Return true if s is a palindrome, considering only alphanumeric characters and ignoring case.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Alphanumeric means letters and digits — so I keep digits too, not just letters? And everything else, like spaces and punctuation, is skipped, and the comparison is case-insensitive?
Correct — letters and digits count, case-insensitive.
Good — so zero P is false, since the zero and the P are both kept, and they differ. This is the converging two-pointer skeleton again, but comparing instead of swapping.

Let me weigh two ways. I could filter into a clean lowercased string and check it against its reverse — simple, but linear extra space. This problem reminds me of the opposite-direction two-pointer pattern, because a palindrome is just a promise that each pair of ends matches. So: l and r converge in place, skipping non-alphanumeric characters on each side and comparing the lowercased ends. Linear time, constant space — no filtered copy.

Here's the plan. One: start l at zero and r at the last index. Two: while l is less than r, if either end isn't alphanumeric, move just that pointer and loop again. Three: compare the lowercased ends; a mismatch returns false, a match moves both inward. Order matters — the two skips come before the compare, so I only ever compare two confirmed alphanumeric characters. Surviving until the pointers meet means it's a palindrome. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me write it. Two skip checks, then one compare, inside a single while loop; falling out of the loop returns true. One detail worth flagging — each continue moves just one pointer and re-enters the loop, which re-checks l less than r, so both ends get aligned onto alphanumeric characters before any comparison, and the pointers never cross mid-skip. For non-ASCII input I'd cast to unsigned char before calling isalnum, but the input is printable ASCII here.

Let's dry-run capital A, space, b, comma, a — which filters to a, b, a, so expected true. The ends match once lowercased, then the space and the comma are skipped one pointer at a time. The row that matters is the last: both pointers land on the b at index two, l less than r is false, so the loop stops and returns true. That matches. Corner cases: zero P is false, a digit against a letter. Dot comma is true — everything is skipped, and an empty string is a palindrome. A single character is true.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear — every loop pass moves at least one pointer, so each character is visited at most once by either pointer. Space is constant — two indices, no filtered copy. Oh, one more thing — this is the same converging skeleton with the middle step changed from swap to compare. Allow deleting one character on a mismatch, trying each side, and it becomes the almost-palindrome variant; the same converging-compare idea underlies the whole family.

Nicely done. Three things stood out: catching that digits count, so zero P is false; skipping before comparing; and choosing the constant-space in-place approach over the filtered-copy version. Good work.
